mhm_organizationName: United States of America Citizen Science
mhm_Comments: This body of water is a 5-6 inch deep puddle formed at the bottom of a recently excavated hole created for the purpose of performing maintenance on a series of pipes used to transport water from my house to a nearby garden. Although this hole has been around for a few weeks and has had a considerable amount of water in it before, it was only within the last few days of consistent rainfall that female mosquitoes have been able to lay eggs in this hole with a guarantee that they would hatch before the water would evaporate or be soaked into the ground. No algae was found in the hole and there were very few areas in this puddle to provide shade for the larvae, but nonetheless, a large population of these larvae were able to survive thanks to their diet of deceased insects and decaying leaves that had also ended up in the water they were raised in. After further analysis and research, I was able to identify it as being either Aedes albopictus or Aedes aegyptii. Afterwards, I used a bucket to remove as much water and mosquito larvae as I could until a very minuscule amount of water and larvae remained (these larvae will quite unlikely reach the pupal or adult stages of their lives due to the water’s quickly decreasing volume and quickly increasing temperature).

mhm_Comments: This body of water is a small, murky pond with an abundance of water plants to provide shade and nursery areas for developing mosquito larvae. However, after taking a number of water samples from the sites, no mosquito larvae found to be present. Despite the seemingly hospitable loving conditions provided for mosquito larvae, a probable answer to their absence most likely lies in the fact that the pond itself was stocked with red-eared slider turtles and number of freshwater fish of varying sizes (both of which I would believe to be predators of mosquito larvae and pupae).

mhm_organizationName: United States of America Citizen Science
mhm_Comments: This body of water was located near a concrete storm drain and had a reasonable amount of water, algae and plants within it. Around 5 mosquito larvae and 2 mosquito pupae were identified and I made an attempt to capture some to bring back home for identification. Despite my efforts at capturing the larvae and pupae, I was low on time and proper field equipment, and after several minutes of trying to hunt down the mosquitoes with my small plastic pipette and sample container the mosquito specimens got the best of me with their speed and hiding abilities before I had the chance to acquire any.

mhm_organizationName: United States of America Citizen Science
mhm_Comments: This site is a small, man-made pond located on the property of a large church. Chances are, the water is likely filtered or sterilized by some means as it’s purpose is more or less for visual appeal to the church rather than an actual pond as it was very clean, clear, and had no visible or notable amounts of plants, algae, or animals and no tree cover. Because of this, it is quite unlikely that mosquitoes spawn in such an environment.

mhm_organizationName: United States of America Citizen Science
mhm_Comments: This body of water is characterized as a small drainage ditch connected to a concrete storage drain. Several regions of the site were scattered with growths of filamentous algae and water plants as well as a high abundance of tadpoles, big and small. Due to predation, it is most likely that any mosquito larvae that previously lived in this ditch were killed off by their tadpole predators. In conclusion, it is likely that if there are any mosquito larvae located at this site, all existing specimens would have been too small to observe in the field and they likely will not survive to reach the pupal stage for as long as the tadpoles remain.

mhm_organizationName: United States of America Citizen Science

mhm_Comments: This site is one of the seven traps that I created to evaluate the effectiveness of the oviposition deterrent effects of different mosquito repellent plants on mosquito species local to my area. This trap is labeled as “trap #1,” the geranium trap, and is filled with decaying leaves and grass, as well as rainwater. Previously, I had not noticed any mosquito larvae in this tire trap, however, as of today I was able to identify exactly one mosquito larvae specimen in the tire that had gone unnoticed last time I checked. The physiology of this larvae specimen was consistent with that of the physical characteristics of the same exact mosquito larvae that I found in my lavender trap the day before last (meaning that it is most likely of the genus Culex). However, due to the fact that only one was spotted, this would mean that the specimen observed is not a mosquito larvae, but instead some other form of aquatic insect larvae (as most mosquitoes produce young hundreds at time). I then came to the conclusion that this was indeed a mosquito larvae and that all other larvae but this one specimen had most likely been consumed by some predator.

mhm_Comments: A amostra coletada se tratou de uma área maior em frente da escola. A linda a área encerra aproximadamente cerca de 350 m quadrados. Cada amostra foi nomeada como ponto de coleta (PC) e o número se trata da sequência da amostragem. Nessa primeira coleta não foi possível realizar a identificação e a coleta, uma vez q a lixeira se encontrava lacrada. A temperatura ambiente era de 29° ensolarado sem nuvens. Não houve precipitação no dia anterior a coleta, isto é 25/03/2018. Na praça foram encontrados muitos copos descartáveis, bem como embalagens de salgadinhos. Além disso a praça em questão não apresenta sombreamento na forma de vegetação ou qualquer outro dispositivo.os trabalhos de coleta e identificação foram realizados com alunos dos 6° e 7° anos.

Lembrando q o equipamento utilizado se trata de um estojo cujo funcionamento é a base de reagentes e a escala de verificação apresenta umbrange pequeno de variação, suficiente para perceber se amostra coletada de água se encontra em um pH tendendo a alcalinidade ou tendendo a acidez. mhm_Comments: I haven’t seen any mosquitos moving around here, and it’s a man-made ditch my parents made to curb the growth of bamboo. Unfortunately, it fills up with water every time it rains. Although no mosquitos were present when observing, the shade and still water make it an ideal place for breeding. My parents complain of mosquito bites every time to work in the garden close to the bamboo, so I suspect there should be some mosquito larvae somewhere. There were some small insects on the surface of the water, although they looked more like small flies than mosquitos.

mhm_Comments: These habitats are a continuation of the mosquito breeding experiment at the last log in this location. The containers were upgraded to 5 gallon buckets because the water in the small containers evaporated too quickly. After upgrading from small containers to large ones, I discovered that a nearby family of pigeons had been drinking from the buckets and washing themselves in them. As advised by project mentors, the water was not changed out after the pigeon bathing, but a netting activity is in progress to protect any potential mosquito larvae in the future from the pigeons. Photo #1 is plain tap water bait. Photo #2 is fermented grass bait. Photo #3 is tropical fish food bait. Photo #4 is Timothy hay rabbit food bait. Photo #5 is pond water collected at San Rancho Rafael park.

mhm_Comments: Trap 1: plain waiter bait. Trap 2: grass infusion bait. Trap 3: tropical fish food bait. Trap 4: Timothy hay bait. Trap 5: Rancho San Rafael pond water bait. No larvae or eggs were present; however, there were adult mosquitoes at the traps. One of the adult mosquitoes entered our house. On killing the mosquito I saw it had no blood in it, so I inferred that my traps were not attracting just mosquitoes who had had their blood meals, but mosquitoes in general. Consequently, I had to eliminate the breeding habitat before waiting for eggs or larvae to form, because more and more mosquitoes were entering our home. When I went to record this MHM log, I saw a live adult mosquito resting on the egg laying paddle in Trap 5, the Rancho San Rafael park pond water. Picture 6 is a close up of the mosquito. Throughout my time in Reno and this experiment, I never once saw a mosquito due to the dry Sierra Nevada desert climate here. However, over the last 5 days a smoke cloud from the California fires has enveloped Reno. This cloud effectively created its own weather: humidity rose, temperatures dropped, and slight drizzles occurred throughout the city, all of which is highly unusual for Reno. I believe the smoke cloud’s micro-climate is what prompted the increase in mosquito life in Reno and my traps.
